posts.title: I Built My Own Granola for $70 With REA and Claude Code (Should You Be Worried?)
posts.subtitle: What REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) is, whether you should be worried, how I built my own Granola with Claude Code, and the full cost.
paras: A GitHub repo went from 1,500 stars to 365,000 in under three weeks.
It’s called REA, short for Reverse Engineer Anything. Matthew Berman shared it on X with three words, “Software is done,” and that post now has 3.8 million views.
If that were true, the app you work on every day could be copied by anyone with a laptop and an AI subscription.

So I tested it. I used REA and Claude Code to build my own version of Granola, the AI meeting notes app, and called it Notewell. It transcribes your calls, knows who said what, and turns your rough notes into clean ones.
It took 1 hour 22 minutes and $70.
This guide covers:
What REA is, in plain English
Should you be worried?
How I built Notewell, step by step
Exactly what it cost
Only want the build? Skip to section 3. Prefer video? The full breakdown is on my YouTube:
Two things before we start:
Save this. Read the safety rules in section 2 before you install anything.
Send it to the one person in your team group who forwarded the “software is done” post.
Subscribe now
Share
1. What is REA?
REA is a free, open-source tool that lets AI coding agents look inside apps they don’t have the code for. One command installs it, and it works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and 21 other agents.
Once it’s in, you can ask your agent how a feature in some app works, and it comes back with an answer plus the evidence for it.
How it actually works (in 30 seconds)
You only need three ideas to follow the rest of this post.
1 - Apps are compiled.
When an app ships to you, its code has been turned into something your computer can run and you can’t read. Reverse engineering turns it back into something a person can follow.
2 - REA runs old tools.

The decompilers it uses have been around for years. IDA goes back to the early 1990s, Hopper was on sale by 2012, and the NSA made Ghidra public in 2019. Apps built on web tech, like most Electron desktop apps, need none of that, because REA can read the JavaScript they ship.
3 - REA is a harness.

A harness wraps an AI model with tools and instructions, the way Claude Code wraps Claude. REA puts all those decompilers behind one door, and every claim it makes comes with evidence: the code it read, the strings and function calls it found, and a list of what it couldn’t see.
★ Remember. REA finds and explains. Your AI agent writes the code.
Why everyone is talking about it
REA isn’t new. It started in April 2026 as a small add-on for one Mac decompiler and sat quietly for six months. Then October happened.
4 Oct: about 1,500 stars.
7 Oct: Replit’s CEO, Amjad Masad, posts that AI decompilation will make all software de facto open source. The post doesn’t name REA, but its creator replies under it with the link.
8 Oct: Berman’s “Software is done.”
16 Oct: Perplexity adds REA to its Computer agent, with reverse-engineering tasks free until 31 October.
23 Oct: 365,472 stars.

The same week, “AI cloned Adobe” was going around too. That was a different project called ArtCraft, and it didn’t use REA. The two stories still got merged, and even Decrypt’s headline tied a free Photoshop to REA.
2. Should you be worried?
No. Software isn’t done. I wouldn’t ignore this either, though, and the reason is in what people have actually built with it.
What people have built

REA’s own team picked two small, clean targets. On Aegis, an Android authenticator app, REA narrowed 3,077 code classes down to the one that makes your six-digit login code, and the rebuilt version passed 133 tests. On DX-Ball, a 1996 Windows game, they rebuilt one sound function in five lines of C.
The community went a bit further:
Glide, a free screen recorder with auto-zoom, built by studying Screen Studio.

Ledger Reborn, an accounting app built by studying the QuickBooks trial. Its reports matched the original’s sample numbers to the cent, though its authors say it isn’t a pixel-perfect copy and they wrote the engine themselves.
hexgrab, a colour picker, where REA got 8 of 9 findings right.
Each of these copies a single feature or a small app.
Nobody has cloned a big commercial app end to end.
What the tests say
At least 15 people ran the same task twice, once with REA and once with a normal AI agent. REA clearly won 4 and tied or lost 7. In the other 4 it got closer to the original but took longer.

The clearest win came from SoftsWeb, who rebuilt OpenAI’s Codex CLI against a hidden test. Without REA it scored 75% for $2. With REA it scored 98.5% for $14, because the missing piece was buried inside the compiled file.
MG went the other way. Rebuilding a screen from an iOS app MG had made, the REA run took about 1 hour 12 minutes and $40. The normal agent took about 40 minutes and $12.
And lustoykov got the same right answer both ways. The REA run just used about 5 million tokens to get there, against 1.5 million.
★ Remember. REA helps when the answer is locked inside a compiled app. For web apps and small programs, a normal AI agent mostly gets there alone, and REA costs 1.5 to 3 times more.
But what about...
“Can someone clone my app now?”
A basic version of your features, yes, and much faster than before. The whole product, nobody has managed yet.
Anything that runs on your server can’t be read this way at all. So assume whatever ships to your user’s device can be read, and keep the logic that matters on the server.
“Is it safe to install?”

Be careful with it. REA’s own security doc says it isn’t a sandbox. Apps it opens run with your permissions, and everything it finds goes to whichever AI model you use. In the first week a fake copy went around with a Windows download that one user reported as a trojan.
I didn’t run it on my laptop at all. I used a Claude Code cloud session, which also kept it away from my own files. If you try it:
Use a VPS or a cloud session, never your main machine.
Install only from npm (rea-agents), github.com/morluto/rea or rea.tools.
Ask about one feature at a time. REA’s own maintainer says “reverse this whole app” is the expensive way to use it.
“Can it get things wrong?”
Yes, and quietly. In one test on a sample desktop app, everything REA reported was correct, but it missed all 8 reply messages and all 4 risky security settings, and never mentioned the gap.
“Is it legal?”

Nobody knows yet. No court has ruled on AI-assisted reverse engineering, and many apps’ terms forbid it. REA’s own disclaimer says to use it only on software you own or are allowed to examine. I’m not a lawyer.
“What does this mean for my career?”
If you’re a student, a “clone of X” project won’t make you stand out anymore, because cloning just got much easier. Build something that solves a real problem for real users.
If you’re an engineer, expect the interview question to move from “can you build this?” to “do you know why it was built this way, with this stack?”
If you’re a founder, features alone won’t protect you. I think data is the real moat now, along with users, trust and distribution.
The rest of this post is for paid subscribers: every step of my build, what Notewell can and can’t do, and the exact bill.

posts.title: 105 ChatGPT photo codes: one photo, one word
posts.subtitle: The 5 codes from my reel, the two prompts that turned my photos into a video, and 100 more to try.
paras: Hi guys, Nishant here. If you commented “gpt” on my reel, this is the list I promised.

A code is a short word you type after uploading a photo of yourself. It tells ChatGPT where the camera stands, what lens it has and what the light is doing. You stay the same person in every result. The picture around you changes completely.
There’s no hidden command list behind the slash. ChatGPT reads the word as a style and works out the rest, which is why a made-up code like /impossibleangle works at all.
The 5 from my reel
All five came from the same photo: me in a pink shirt, at night, by the water. I uploaded it, typed the code, and sent it. Nothing else went in the prompt.
/impossibleangle: a selfie from a spot no camera could reach. Mine put me on the edge of a tower, arm stretched out, with the whole city lit up below.
/droneview: shot from straight above. You look up into the lens and the ground becomes the background.
/fisheye: a round, bulging lens. The skyline bent all the way around me.
/wormview: the camera sits on the floor and points up. My shoes ended up as the biggest thing in the frame.

/coverstory: turns the photo into a magazine cover. ChatGPT wrote the headlines from what it already knew about me, starting with my name and “From Microsoft to a Multi-Million Creator & Founder”. If yours gets the details wrong, add them after the code, for example /coverstory name: Priya, headline: the designer who quit to build her own studio.
If someone you know posts photos of themselves, send them this.
Subscribe now
Photos to video: the storyboard trick
My second reel took the same idea one step further. It used two prompts in two apps.
Step 1, in ChatGPT. Upload a photo of yourself and paste this:

Create a storyboard image for my video edit cuts every second for photoshootIt came back with 24 frames on one sheet, one shot per second. Each frame has a timestamp and a direction: smile to camera, look right, hair touch, feet close up, walk towards, laugh, back shot, end wide shot.
Step 2, in Gemini. Start a new chat. Attach the storyboard plus a few more photos of you, so it sees your face from more than one angle. I attached four. Then paste this:

Create a cinematic UGC style video according to the storyboard. Keep the character consistent according to the other images attachedGemini said it would take a few minutes. The video that came back followed the sheet: the smile, the hair touch, the walk along the railing.
Yes the video in Gemini is free, if you were thinking.
100 more to try

The five above are the ones from my reel. I haven’t shown results for the other hundred, so treat them as a list to try. Type them the same way: photo first, then the code. If a result misses, add a few plain words after the code saying what you wanted.
📐 Where the camera is
/topdown: straight down while you lie on grass, sand or a bed, with your hair and clothes spread out around you.
/lowangle: from just below your chin, looking up. You look taller and more sure of yourself.
/overshoulder: from behind you, looking at what you’re looking at, like a view, a laptop or a crowd.
/sideprofile: your face from the side, against a plain wall or the sky.
/backshot: from behind as you face a view. You become the thing that shows how big the scene is.
/mirrorselfie: taken in a mirror with the phone in shot. It works best when the room is interesting.
/cafewindow: from outside a café window, with the street reflected across the glass.
/closeup: your face fills the frame. Start from a sharp photo for this one.
/tinyinframe: you, very small, in a wide valley or an empty street.
/handheldpov: your own hands in shot, holding a coffee, a ticket or a phone.
🔭 Lens and focus
/portraitlens: face sharp, background melted away. The classic portrait look.
/widelens: takes in the whole room or street, with a slight stretch at the edges.
/telephoto: shot from far away on a long lens, so the background looks huge and close behind you.
/bokehlights: the lights behind you turn into soft round blobs. Best at night.
/tiltshift: the whole scene looks like a miniature model.
/macro: very close detail, like your watch, an eye or the weave of a shirt.
/anamorphic: a wide cinema frame with long horizontal lens flares.
/zoomblur: streaks pulling out from the centre, as if the lens zoomed mid-shot.
💡 Light
/goldenhour: low, warm sun and long shadows. Flattering on almost everyone.
/bluehour: just after sunset, with a deep blue sky and streetlights coming on.
/harshflash: direct phone flash in the dark, with the background gone black. Party photo.
/windowlight: soft light from one window, half your face in gentle shadow.
/neonnight: shop signs washing pink and blue light over your skin.
/backlight: the sun behind you and a glow around your hair.
/silhouette: only your outline, black against a bright sky.
/candlelit: warm, low and flickering. Dinner-table mood.
/overcast: flat grey daylight with no harsh shadows. Calm and real.
/lowkey: mostly darkness with one light source on you.
/sunbeams: visible rays coming through trees or a dusty window.
/screenglow: lit only by a laptop or phone screen in a dark room.
🌦️ Time and weather
/rainynight: wet streets that double every light.
/fog: soft grey air, with the background fading out behind you.
/snowfall: flakes in the air and on your shoulders.
/sunrise: pale pink sky and empty streets.
/midnight: a late, empty city under orange streetlights.
/stormclouds: a dark, heavy sky behind you while you stay brightly lit.
/autumnleaves: orange and red trees, with leaves on the ground.
/desertdusk: sand dunes in the last warm light of the day.
/cherryblossom: pink trees overhead and petals on the path.
🎞️ Film and era
/35mm: film grain and warmer colour, like a print from a photo lab.
/polaroid: square, with a white border and faded colour.
/disposable: cheap-camera flash and slightly crooked framing.
/vhsstill: a paused frame from an old home video, with scan lines and smeared colour.
/earlydigital: the look of a 2005 point-and-shoot, with blown-out highlights and grainy shadows.
/bwportrait: black and white with deep contrast. Serious and classic.
/70sfilm: warm, faded colour from a family album.
/photobooth: a strip of four frames from a mall photo booth.
/daguerreotype: a stiff portrait on a metal plate from the 1800s.
🎨 Colour
/tealorange: warm skin and cool shadows, the blockbuster grade.
/pastel: soft, low-saturation colour everywhere.
/fadedfilm: lifted blacks and washed-out colour.
/vividpop: very saturated, almost cartoon colour.
/earthtones: browns, olives and creams only.
/blackwhitered: black and white, with one red thing in the frame.
/duotone: two colours only, like a gig poster.
📰 Covers and posters
These work the same way /coverstory does. Add your name or a title after the code if you want specific text on it.
/albumcover: your photo as a music album cover, with a title and artist name.
/movieposter: a film poster with your name above the title and credits along the bottom.
/bookcover: a paperback cover with you on the front.
/wantedposter: an old Western wanted poster with your face on it.
/tradingcard: a sports trading card, with your stats on the back.
/stamp: your portrait on a postage stamp.
/billboard: your photo on a giant billboard above a city street.
/newspaperfront: the front page of a newspaper, with you as the main story.
🎤 Scenes for your profile
/keynotestage: you on a big conference stage with your name on the screen behind you.
/podcastguest: a podcast studio with a microphone, headphones and warm light.
/linkedinheadshot: a clean, well-lit headshot in a blazer against a plain background.
/officecandid: at a desk mid-laugh, with colleagues blurred behind you.
/redcarpet: premiere night, a logo wall behind you and cameras flashing.
/streetstyle: a street-fashion photographer caught you mid-walk.
🎬 Genre
/filmstill: a paused frame from a film, with black bars top and bottom.
/noir: black and white, with window-blind shadows across you, like a 1940s detective film.
/scifi: a neon city in the rain, with a future skyline behind you.
/sportsaction: frozen mid-sprint or mid-jump, the way a sports photographer would catch it.
/concertstage: you on stage lit from behind, with the crowd in front.
/travelpostcard: a vintage postcard of the place you’re in, with you in it.
/heistmovie: a dark suit, a briefcase, and a crew walking behind you.
🏃 Motion
/midjump: caught at the top of a jump.
/hairflip: hair mid-swing, face still sharp.
/rushhour: you standing still on a busy platform while everyone around you blurs.
/candidlaugh: mid-laugh, eyes half closed, nothing posed.
/splash: water frozen in the air around you.
/walktowards: walking at the camera with one foot mid-step.
🖌️ Turn it into art
/museumpainting: your photo as an oil painting in a gallery frame, with a small label beside it.
/watercolor: a soft watercolour painting.
/pencilsketch: a graphite sketch on paper.
/3dcartoon: you as a character from an animated film.
/claymation: you as a clay figure from a stop-motion film.
/pixelart: a 16-bit video game character.
/comicpanel: you in a comic strip, with speech bubbles.
/stickerset: a sheet of six stickers of you, each with a different expression.
/actionfigure: you as a boxed toy figure, with accessories in the packaging.
/popart: four bright repeats of your face in a grid.
✂️ Edit your photo
/nightversion: the same photo and pose, at night.
/agedup: you at 70.
/suitup: the same photo, in a tailored suit.
/teleport: the same pose, dropped into another city. Put the city after the code.
/removecrowd: clears the people out from behind you.
/fixlighting: the same photo, relit as if a photographer had set up lights.
/fourseasons: a 2×2 grid of you in spring, summer, autumn and winter.
/expressions: six versions of your face on one sheet: laughing, serious, surprised and more.
Using two at once

Start with one code. If you add a second, make it the light: /wormview /bluehour or /closeup /windowlight. With three or more, the styles start to fight each other. When a result looks muddy, go back to one code and change only that.
Which one should I try on the next reel? Reply with the code.
Subscribe now

posts.title: I edit every video with Claude. Here are all my skills.
posts.subtitle: The exact setup behind my reels and my YouTube long-form: the tools, the 10-stage pipeline, nine edit formats, and the 25 skills that run it. Paid subscribers get every file.
paras: Hi guys, Nishant here.

If you came from my latest video: yes, that whole 16-minute video was edited by Claude. I shot it. Claude cut it from the raw footage, removed the dead air and my fumbles, synced my screen recordings to the camera, built every graphic, placed every sound effect and rendered it. Then a second model reviewed the render before I was allowed to see it.

In one line: Claude edits every video I post, a different model reviews it, and every mistake becomes a rule it never repeats. This post is the full setup. Paid subscribers get the 25 skills that run it.
Watch the video (16:22):
In this post:
What it costs (less than you think)
The 10-stage pipeline every edit goes through
My nine edit formats
The three things that actually made the edits good
How to teach Claude any editing style
For paid subscribers: all 25 skills, the install guide and the exact prompts I use
Subscribe now
This video, cut by cut
Here’s what “Claude edited it” actually means. Every bar below is one cut in the video: 205 of them over 16 minutes, each one placed, styled and timed by Claude.

I’m making three to four reels a day the same way. A human editor plus a motion designer would take one to one and a half days for one of my reels; Claude delivers it in under two hours. My podcast clips are cut automatically in Codex and Claude Code.
What it costs
$20 a month. A Claude Pro or a ChatGPT Plus subscription. In India that’s about ₹2,000 a month.
Every editor I use is free to start:
HyperFrames by HeyGen. Open source. The video is HTML and animation code, so an agent can write all of it. My long-form and vlogs are built here now.
Remotion. Video as React code. Free for individuals and teams of up to three.
Palmier Pro. An AI-native editor for Mac, driven through its MCP server.
DaVinci Resolve, through a community MCP server.
Pick one. The skills work with any of them.
Why skills
A skill is a set of instructions Claude follows when you give it a task. That’s all it is: a folder with a markdown file in it, sometimes a few scripts.
The model is already smart. What it doesn’t have is your taste and your mistakes. My skills are mostly rules it got wrong exactly once, written down so it never gets them wrong again.

“Registers hard-cut, never crossfade” is in there because a crossfade shipped and looked broken. “Never zoom at a cut” is in there because I said “this shows that there is a cut” twice. Every rule has its reason next to it.
The 10-stage pipeline
Every edit goes through the same ten stages, in this order. Each stage is its own skill.
The three that most people skip are the ones that matter most:
Asset plan (stage 0). Before a single cut, every visual is classified and every claim I make is fact-checked against the live page. Nothing starts until I say yes.
Cut audit (stage 2). The transcript is not evidence, because speech recognition hides a repeated phrase. This stage checks the audio itself.
Review gate (stage 9). A different model watches the render and lists what’s broken. I only see the video after it passes.
Nine edit formats
Each format is its own skill, with its own measured layout. A router skill reads what I ask for and picks one, so I can just say “edit this reel”.
The three things that actually made it good

1. The model that edits is not the model that reviews. A model grading its own work passes its own work. Quality didn’t move until I split those two jobs. My edits run on Claude Opus; the review runs on a different model that looks at frames from every section. And every note I give goes back into a skill.

2. Check the audio, not the transcript. On my first draft of this video, a few cuts sounded abrupt. A full sweep found 15 lines where the cut ended at the start of the last word instead of its end. “Edited using AI” played as “edited using”. “Absolutely free” played as “absolutely”. Every check had passed, because every check asked “is there speech at the edge?” instead of “is a word cut in half?”.
The fix went into the rough-cut skill as a rule and a script that checks every edge, so it can’t happen again.

3. Every correction becomes a rule. When I say “the bubble is too zoomed in” or “my face should be on the left because I’m looking right”, it fixes the video and updates the skill. After a few weeks the corrections get rare.
Teach it any style
This is my favourite part. Give Claude a video you like and ask it to learn the edit.

It watches the reference at two frames per second with the watch skill, reads the transcript, and measures everything. On one reference it found 31% of the time was full face, 24% split screen and 45% a full canvas with no face. It writes that into a style document, then into a new skill. My Paper Drawer and Whiteout formats were born exactly like that.
You can do the same with colour grading, typography, animations, anything you can point at.
What it still can’t do

It’s an assistant editor, not a button. I still shoot everything, approve the asset plan, and give notes after the first draft. On this video my notes were things like “this cut is abrupt”, “move the video a little right so the text has room” and “reduce the sound effects by 4 dB”. It took three rounds of notes.
But I never opened a timeline.
What paid subscribers get
Everything above is the what and the why. Below the paywall is the how: the actual files.

posts.title: How I Sold my First Company at 25
posts.subtitle: From a student to a software engineer to actually building and selling my first company.
paras: Let’s be completely honest: I never actually wanted to be a software engineer. I just wanted to make money.

The story starts way before the company did back when I was in my 11th standard preparing for the JEE. For those unfamiliar, the JEE is the gateway to India’s best engineering colleges, and the competition is cutthroat. Every single year, nearly 1 million students appear for it. Across all government-backed engineering colleges in India, there are only about 50,000 seats. If you just look at computer science? You’re fighting for one of roughly 10,000 spots in a pool of a million people.
Nishant's Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Around that time, I saw a news piece about seven students from a college in Delhi called NSIT who bagged $120k packages at Google Mountain View. (Most people haven’t heard of NSIT because it isn’t an IIT or NIT, but it is incredibly prestigious). It was 2015, and $120,000 felt like an unimaginable amount of money. I didn’t know what competitive programming was, I didn’t know the tech landscape, but I made my decision right there: I was going to study computer science at NSIT.
The Road to Microsoft
I got into NSIT, put my head down, and worked hard for four years. That hustle landed me an internship at Samsung and a campus placement at Cult.fit.
But then Covid hit.

My offer got delayed, so I had to pivot and start applying off-campus. That forced detour turned out to be a blessing in disguise, leading directly to a role at Microsoft. That’s how my actual software engineering journey began.
Accidental Content Creator

During my final year of university, I decided to give YouTube a shot. I grew up watching MKBHD, Mrwhosetheboss, and Unbox Therapy. Initially, my grand plan was just to become a tech YouTuber so I could get free gadgets to review. But I had no money and zero following, so no brand was going to send me free tech.
So, I sat down and asked myself: What do I actually know?

Funny enough, my very first video was a painting of a sunset. Predictably, it got zero views. So I pivoted. I had just cracked the Cult.fit placement, and back in 2020, there wasn’t a lot of tech placement content on YouTube. Inspired by creators like Sing in USA (Harnoor), I decided to host Zoom-recorded podcast interviews.

I recorded about 30 podcast episodes and scraped my way to 1,000 subscribers. Around that time, I connected with Love Babbar, a college senior who completely changed my trajectory. He mentored me on the mechanics of YouTube—why my current strategy wasn’t working, the psychology of titles and thumbnails, the importance of the video’s hook, and how to position myself.
I took his advice, implemented everything, and in just three months, my channel skyrocketed from 1,000 to 10,000 subscribers.
The 30-Day Challenge
Right around hitting 10k subs, I got my offer from Microsoft. I knew that once I started my corporate job, I might never have the time to go all-in on content again.

So, I committed to a massive challenge: 30 long-form videos in 30 days. No shorts, no Reels, just pure, daily long-form content. I didn’t stress about finding a perfect “niche”; I just went with the flow and posted consistently.

By the end of those 30 days, right as I was joining Microsoft, my channel blew up. People started asking for interview advice, MS prep strategies, and behind-the-scenes looks at my life as a software engineer. When my office shifted to a hybrid model, I documented my move to Hyderabad and my apartment hunt. People loved the authenticity, and to this day, I try to keep that exact same raw energy on camera.
Building AlgoPrep

One day, I got a message from Subhash. He was a popular instructor at PepCoding (which was later acquired by Scaler), and many of my friends had actually learned Data Structures and Algorithms from him.

Subhash had just landed an offer from Amazon Germany, but he still had a deep passion for teaching. He reached out to me with a pitch: “I’m going to Amazon Germany, but I still want to teach. You have the distribution. Let’s build something together.”

I hesitated. I love mentoring and interacting with people, but I never wanted to be an EdTech founder or create courses because I didn’t have a burning passion for the teaching side of it. I took some time, talked to my friends and family, and eventually figured, why not?
We launched AlgoPrep. This was my first real company. In less than a year and a half, we scaled the platform to 100,000 free users and 7,000 paid users.
The Acquisition

At the same time, the EdTech sector was heating up again. Companies were realizing that traditional college curriculums were moving too slowly to keep up with industry tech. A new wave of “alt colleges” emerged, looking to bridge that gap by having actual industry experts teach the skills companies actually wanted.
We had built exactly what they needed.

Multiple companies reached out wanting to acquire us. A few deals fell through, but eventually, Sunstone acquired AlgoPrep to help launch the Vedam School of Technology. Because of NDAs, I can’t disclose the exact numbers, but it was a great deal structured over a three-year payout.
Knowing When to Walk Away
Post-acquisition, I joined Sunstone as Assistant Vice President and Head of Product, working directly with the founder, Piyush. The exposure was incredible, and I learned an immense amount.
But a few months in, reality hit me. This wasn’t what I wanted to do for the rest of my life. It wasn’t my true calling.
I walked into Piyush’s office and told him the truth. We parted ways on great terms.

Around the same time, I received an offer to join Entrepreneur First for their fall cohort. Today, my social media audience has grown to 1.5 million across platforms. I get to do what I love: tell stories, create content, and build my next venture a consumer AI company.
But more on that later.

notes.body:
Made this out of a 3hr long podcast. Where claude decided the clips and then edited it too. 

All this was done in less than 2hrs, and now it’s a repeatable skill. 

Wrote a substack article on this! Go check it out :)

My Instagram video editor is not a human anymore.

I have created a workflow to edit all my videos, all the motion graphics, and b-rolls, and everything is done using AI. 

Still, the person who is creating these videos. If you want to understand how I do this, do subscribe to my Substack. 

I'm planning to write an article on this, and I'll also share the skills that I've created specifically for my project so that it works like how it works.

New to the platform. So just a short introduction about myself. 

I am Nishant, currently building Miles, your personal shopping assistant. I was part of Entrepreneurs First and raised a pre-seed from them! 

Before that I built Algoprep, which got acquired by a series d company. 

Before that worked at Microsoft for 3 years. In Parallel i created content, grew it to a following of 1.5 million. 

I want to connect with founders and builders.
